subsystems.name: Trait genetics
subsystems.role: identifies which genes set an appearance trait, and whether one edit could plausibly shift it.

subsystems.name: Editor design
subsystems.role: the molecular tool that rewrites a specific DNA letter without cutting the genome apart.

subsystems.name: Delivery
subsystems.role: gets the editor into the intended cells of skin, cartilage or bone — the hardest unsolved step.
parts: electroporation for cells edited outside the body

subsystems.name: Cell targeting
subsystems.role: restricts editing to one cell type, so blood, nerve or germline cells are not altered.

subsystems.name: Control and reversal
subsystems.role: keeps an edit switchable, since appearance changes are permanent and patients may want them undone.

subsystems.name: Safety and monitoring
subsystems.role: measures unintended edits and immune reactions before and after treatment.

buildSteps.title: Choose a trait and a gene
buildSteps.detail: Pick something close to a single gene — melanin pigmentation, hair form, or a bone-density pathway like LRP5 — rather than height or face shape, which involve hundreds of variants and strong environmental effects.

buildSteps.title: Confirm causality
buildSteps.detail: Check that the variant really changes the trait in human data, not just in mice, since almost every appearance trait is polygenic.

buildSteps.title: Design the editor
buildSteps.detail: Write a guide RNA against the target sequence and adapt a base editor or prime editor to make the desired change without a double-strand break.

buildSteps.title: Test in cells and animals
buildSteps.detail: Edit skin fibroblasts, keratinocytes or cartilage cells in culture, then test local injection in animal models and measure the resulting trait change.

buildSteps.title: Solve delivery to the target tissue
buildSteps.detail: Package the editor in lipid nanoparticles or a tissue-tropic viral vector, or inject directly into the dermis — deep tissues such as bone are far harder to reach than the liver, which lipid nanoparticles already reach well.

buildSteps.title: Interrogate safety
buildSteps.detail: Sequence the whole genome to count off-target edits, check for immune reactions to the editor protein, and confirm no germline cells are affected.

buildSteps.title: Prove it in a medical indication first
buildSteps.detail: The route to practice runs through disease: gene editing for skin-blistering disorders, scarring or bone disease would establish the safety record that cosmetic use would later borrow.

buildSteps.title: Scale and regulate
buildSteps.detail: Move from one-off dosing to a manufactured, quality-controlled product, then obtain approval for a use that is optional rather than medically necessary.

prerequisites.why: a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle-cell disease reached approval in 2023, proving edited cells can be given safely in at least one setting.
lipid nanoparticles reliably reach the liver, but skin, cartilage and bone targeting remain research-stage.

prerequisites.tech: Trait genetics precise enough to predict outcomes
prerequisites.why: most appearance traits are polygenic, so a single edit usually gives a modest, uncertain change.
no approved system lets a clinician tune or switch off an edit already made in the body.
edits must be confined to the patient's own body cells, never eggs, sperm or embryos.

pathway.milestone: approved ex-vivo editing of blood cells for disease; early trials of in-vivo editing of the liver
pathway.unlocks: a real clinical and regulatory template for editing human cells.

pathway.milestone: local, in-vivo editing for a medical skin or bone condition
pathway.unlocks: evidence that delivery to these tissues works and persists.

pathway.milestone: editors with dose control and off-switches, plus long-term safety data
pathway.unlocks: the reversibility that an optional cosmetic procedure would require.

pathway.milestone: heavily regulated cosmetic use limited to a few near-single-gene traits
pathway.unlocks: permanent changes to pigmentation, hair form or local fat distribution — but not to height, face shape or anything strongly polygenic, which would remain out of reach.
